column1: What is 'Vibe Coding' as defined by Andrej Karpathy, and how does it differ from traditional code completion tools like IntelliSense?
column2: Vibe Coding is a workflow where a human directs an LLM via natural language prompts to generate/refactor code, acting as architect/intent-clarifier rather than line-by-line author. Unlike IntelliSense (token-level completion), the human operates at the intent/specification layer, not the syntax layer.

column1: In Vibe Coding, what are the four defining architectural roles/steps in the workflow?
column2: 1) Natural language as the primary interface, 2) LLM as the code synthesis engine, 3) Human as the semantic oracle (evaluates correctness/security/fit), 4) Iterative refinement via subsequent prompts.

column1: Why does changing a tensor's stride tuple (e.g., via transpose) avoid copying memory, and when does a copy become necessary?
column2: Strides encode byte offsets per axis, so reinterpreting the same underlying memory with new strides achieves zero-copy transposition/reshaping. A copy becomes necessary when the tensor is non-contiguous and must be passed to a BLAS/CUDA kernel requiring contiguous memory, triggered via `.contiguous()`.

column1: What is the formula for element z_ij in matrix multiplication z = x @ y where x ∈ ℝ^(M×K), y ∈ ℝ^(K×N)?
column2: z_ij = Σ_{k=1}^{K} x_ik · y_kj — an inner product over K values, dispatched to BLAS level-3 GEMM kernels (cuBLAS, oneDNN/MKL, rocBLAS) which tile computation to fit cache hierarchies.

column1: What determines whether an LLM inference workload is memory-bound or compute-bound in the roofline model?
column2: Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte of memory traffic) compared against the hardware's ridge point (peak compute throughput ÷ peak memory bandwidth). Below the ridge point = memory-bound; above = compute-bound.

column1: Why is the decode phase of autoregressive LLM inference catastrophically memory-bound while prefill is compute-bound?
column2: Decode: each weight is read once per token for one MAC op (~2 FLOPs/byte), ~148x below the H100 ridge point (~295 FLOPs/byte) — ALUs sit idle waiting on HBM. Prefill: weights are reused across all p prompt tokens (~2p FLOPs/byte), exceeding the ridge point when p > ~148, making it compute-bound.

column1: What is the hard physical ceiling formula for decode-phase token throughput, and why can't software optimization exceed it?
column2: decode_throughput ≈ HBM_bandwidth / total_weight_bytes. It is a hard ceiling because the bottleneck is DRAM speed, not computation — no kernel fusion, CUDA graphs, or scheduling can exceed the physical rate at which weights can be streamed from HBM.

column1: What is the key architectural difference explaining why vLLM and TensorRT-LLM use separate execution paths for prefill vs. decode?
column2: Prefill is compute-bound and benefits from large batched GEMM kernels optimized for tensor cores; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and uses memory-optimized GEMV kernels instead, since tensor core utilization during decode is effectively zero.

column1: In the 'semantic compilation model' of vibe coding, how does probabilistic LLM-based compilation differ from traditional deterministic compilation?
column2: Traditional compilation (lexing, parsing, type checking, codegen) is a pure deterministic function. LLM-based 'compilation' of natural language intent to code is probabilistic: it samples token sequences via P(output|c,p) = Π P(w_t | w_<t, c, p; θ), so identical prompts can yield different code outputs.

column1: What effect does temperature (τ) have on LLM token sampling, and what is the formula?
column2: P(w_t=k) = exp(logit_k/τ) / Σ_j exp(logit_j/τ). As τ→0, sampling becomes greedy (argmax/deterministic); at τ=1, sampling draws from the raw softmax distribution, introducing non-determinism in generated code.

column1: Per the curriculum's primary lever for output quality, what matters more than prompt phrasing in vibe coding, and why?
column2: Context management matters more than prompt phrasing, because the attention mechanism assigns relevance weights across all context tokens; the signal-to-noise ratio of the context determines whether attention concentrates on information needed for correct code or diffuses across irrelevant tokens.

column1: Why must training loops and evaluation loops be architecturally separate in PyTorch, and what happens if evaluation runs in training mode?
column2: Training loop (`model.train()`) builds an autograd DAG, applies Dropout masking, and uses mini-batch BatchNorm statistics. Evaluation loop (`model.eval()` + `torch.no_grad()`) disables autograd, makes Dropout an identity function, and uses running BatchNorm statistics for deterministic output. Evaluating in training mode produces stochastic, batch-size-dependent, non-reproducible and artificially pessimistic metrics.
